messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark is a 54-year-old forester who has worked in the Pacific Northwest for over thirty years, a career that once grounded his sense of purpose and competence. Eighteen months ago, during a routine felling operation, a chain of events he still replays in vivid detail led to a tree he was directional-felling striking a younger crew member, Dan, with such force that Dan’s leg was crushed below the knee. The injury required multiple surgeries and eventually an amputation. Mark was not physically hurt in the moment, but he felt the saw’s recoil in his shoulders as the trunk twisted, and in the frantic minutes that followed he heaved against the fallen timber with his lower back torqued at an awkward angle. That same dull ache in his lower back has never fully left him. When it flares—bending to tie his boot, or lifting a bag of groceries—his body instinctively tenses into the same hunched, straining posture he held that afternoon, and the memory floods back with it: the sound of the saw, Dan’s shout, the sickening weight of the log.

In the first weeks after the accident, Mark found himself unable to sit still at home. He would pace the living room, his jaw clenched, watching the driveway for no one in particular. His wife noticed he flinched when their dog approached from behind; he began scanning the aisles at the hardware store, cataloguing every man who walked in. He could not shake the conviction that strangers posed a latent threat, even in ordinary places like the post office or the gas station. At night, when the house was quiet, he lay rigid, his mind racing with replays of the event. What frightened him most was not the memory itself but the rage that accompanied it—a hot, wordless fury that he sometimes directed at himself, sometimes at no one at all, and that would leave him shaking. And then, just as suddenly, grief would overtake him: a heavy, sinking sorrow for Dan, for the life Dan had lost, for the fact that Mark had done it.

Mark had always believed that responsibility for a mistake meant examining your own choices. But as weeks turned into months, that belief warped into something darker. He became certain that something inside him—some flaw he could not name—had made the accident happen. He began to doubt his own judgment in small decisions, second-guessing the lean of a tree or the placement of his feet. The thought that he could no longer trust himself spread like a crack through a windshield. By the time the company offered him a desk-based role, he turned it down; he could not imagine doing any job that once defined him, because he was no longer a man who could be counted on. He stopped accepting invitations from friends, avoided the diner where he used to grab coffee with colleagues, and began driving a longer route home to bypass the stretch of forest road where the logging camp was visible.

Today, Mark arrives for his first therapy appointment with his wife waiting in the car. He has lost nearly fifteen pounds, sleeps in fits, and has not worked in six months. He came because his wife said she could not watch him disappear piece by piece, but also because a part of him, buried under the shame, still wants to believe he might again feel capable of something. What he is most afraid of—and what he does not say aloud—is that he will sit in this room and confirm what he already knows: that the accident revealed something true about him, and that there is no way back to the man he used to be.
